# **Manifesto**

**Intelligence is going to the price of water. Soon it will be close to free.**

When intelligence is free, a better model makes exclusive data more valuable and makes everyone's public reasoning worthless.

So **value** moves. And it **concentrates in what stays scarce**.

## **What stays scarce**

**When intelligence is water, the scarce thing is the reservoir it flows through,** and the compounding proprietary data that the flow leaves behind.

Analysis of public information converges to the same free commodity for everyone. 

**The only edge that survives is proprietary data** that exists nowhere else  and it only becomes an edge when it is linked to outcomes, so that every past decision teaches the next one.

**That is the asset that gets *stronger* as models improve:** better intelligence extracts more value from your exclusive, outcome-linked data while making everyone else's reasoning free and identical.

## **The buy-side is not ready**

**Investment firms sit on the raw scarce resources —** capital, access, and decades of proprietary decisions. But that **data is dead**. It lives in folders, in spreadsheets, in the heads of partners who leave. It does not compound.

**So the winner is** not whoever has the most proprietary data today. It is **whoever compounds it fastest,** and today no one has the infrastructure to do that. That is the opening.

## **What we build**

**We own the container: the ontology through which free intelligence flows, does the work, and leaves behind proprietary data that compounds into a moat.**

We give firms the infrastructure to accelerate their work at unprecedented speed — free-like intelligence flowing through every workstream  and, as a byproduct of that speed, to generate the outcome-linked data that makes every future decision more accurate.

**Coordination work disappears. Judgment stays human** because someone must still be accountable for capital, and accountability does not transfer to a model no matter how good it gets. But that judgment is now served with all the analysis it could ever need, and every judgment it makes is captured, linked to its outcome, and fed back.

**We are the place where agents and humans get the work done naturally  with total visibility and a truth-seeking engine that keeps the process honest and moving.**

## **The one idea**

**Being the place where work gets done, and being the place where proprietary data compounds.**

The firm does not have to build a data asset. They just have to do their work  faster and better than they ever could before. The compounding is the exhaust of that work. The moat builds itself, while they simply do their job.

**That is what we are building: the reservoir for the buy-side, in the moment intelligence becomes water.**

## **The data taxonomy**

The word "data" is hiding five completely different things, and the critical insight is that they have *different scarcity and different compounding behavior*. 

**Category 1 — Inbound raw material.** The decks, VDR contents, management models, etc Everyone receives it, it's about the company not about the investment company and all your competitors who have access to the deal receive it. 

**Category 2 — Methodology / templates.** The pre-built LBO model, the B2B SaaS model, the cap-table template, the valuation framework, the diligence checklist. This is the firm's *way of working* — the 80% shared across firms plus the 20% specific to yours. It's reusable structure. It compounds weakly (it improves as you refine templates) but it's largely copyable and it's the part a good model will increasingly generate itself. Semi-scarce, semi-durable.

**Category 3 — Generated analysis. Your own model, your valuation, your competitive research, your market maps.** Today this is the associate's output — the scarce, expensive thing. In the free-intelligence world this becomes *nearly worthless* because the model generates it. It does not compound and it does not stay scarce. This is the category that's collapsing, and any product whose value is "we generate this faster" dies.

**Category 4 — Proprietary interaction data.** The expert calls, the customer references, the founder conversations, the management meetings, the *content* of what was actually said to you, that exists nowhere else because you were in the room and no one else was. A customer telling you "we'd churn if the founder left" is proprietary, outcome-relevant, and un-derivable. This is genuinely scarce and it's yours. It compounds if structured. This is a real part of the reservoir.

**Category 5 — Proprietary judgment-and-outcome data. The scarcest and most valuable, and the one no one captures today: *what your firm decided, why, against what alternatives, who dissented, and what actually happened.*** The IC recordings where the decision got made. The partner's reasoning. The stance that turned out right or wrong. Linked to the eventual MOIC**.** This is the only category that compounds indefinitely and strengthens as models improve, because it's the firm's judgment function made into data, and it exists nowhere on earth except inside your firm's own history.

* Category 1 flows in, free intelligence turns it into Category 3 as exhaust and  
* Categories 4 and 5 get captured as a byproduct.   
* Category 2 is the configurable methodology layer that makes it feel native to each firm. Great operating value. 

## **Deal as a living body**

**Continuity of understanding between decisions changes radically. The decisions stay human and discrete; the knowing becomes continuous and machine-maintained.**

**Today's world is discrete in *understanding*, not just decisions.** 

* Knowledge exists only in scattered snapshots, each held by a different person.  
* There is no continuous state of the deal, there is a set of disconnected fragments, and the only place they ever integrate is imperfectly, temporarily, in the deal lead's overloaded head.   
* Between decision points, understanding *decays*,  people forget, context is lost at handoffs, the memo written at the end is a reconstruction, not a live truth.

**The new world is discrete in *decisions* but continuous in understanding.** T

* The deal is a living body whose understanding is always integrated, always current, always complete, and visible to everyone at once.   
* Intelligence flows through it constantly, so between the human decision points the understanding never decays, it deepens.   
* The human still decides discretely, but they decide against a continuously-maintained, fully-integrated state instead of against fragments they scramble to assemble. 

Claude \+ MCP requires you to formulate the question. But that's precisely the problem: you don't know when there's something you should know.

**The OS doesn't wait for the question.** When the plan extract reveals that 54.3% of the pipeline is unnamed, the system already recognizes this as a pattern it has seen in other deals, and surfaces that insight right then and there, tied to that specific uncertainty.

The difference isn't in the answer—it's that the answer arrives before you even know you need to ask the question. P**ull becomes push, triggered at the exact moment when the context makes it relevant.**

**Memory isn't an archive of deals; it's an archive of evidence organized by type of question.**

**Having the one insight that's genuinely useful—the one you would never have thought to ask for—exactly where it's needed.**

**The OS operates on standing context rather than user-initiated prompts.** It maintains an event-driven orchestration layer over a federated ontology: when a material event occurs — a new artifact, a changed assumption — the system *resolves what that event implies*, traverses the entity graph to retrieve relevant evidence wherever it lives (a 2022 deal folder, an IC note from three years ago, an M\&A comp), invokes external systems through agentic API calls (Mergermarket, CapIQ, web research) under a permission and policy layer, composes multi-agent workflows, and surfaces the result *bound to the open question it answers* — flagging precisely where human judgment is required. The user never queries. 

The system proposes, and the human adjudicates. This requires: an ontology (semantic layer), an event bus, a policy/permission protocol defining what agents may do autonomously vs. what requires approval (the rails), and an audit trail binding every action to its provenance

**It keeps track of everything that's happening across all workstreams, in context. Or, depending on the emphasis. Not "what blocks what" as a list. Where uncertainties converge.**

**What should happen next, who does it, in what sequence, with what authority, and how the result is verified.**
